speaker: fitz
text: In 1861, Chicago set out to lift this six-story brick hotel six feet into the air.

speaker: fitz
text: It was the Tremont House. The Chicago Tribune reported five hundred men tending about five thousand screw jacks to raise it.

speaker: fitz
text: And it said the hotel stayed open.

speaker: gauge
text: Wait. Why not just... build a new hotel?

speaker: fitz
text: Because the hotel wasn't the problem. The city sat too low to drain.

speaker: fitz
text: And Chicago has been fighting its water ever since.

speaker: gauge
text: A city versus water? Water has never lost. Somebody get me a scoreboard.

speaker: gauge
text: Here's the game. I pitch a fix. If Chicago actually did it, I get a point.

speaker: fitz
text: In the 1850s, Chicago sat on flat, wet prairie, barely above the level of Lake Michigan. In wet seasons, the ground turned to mud.

speaker: fitz
text: The city needed sewers, and sewers work by gravity: the pipe has to slope downhill to the river.

speaker: gauge
text: Easy. Dig the sewers deeper. Fix number one.

speaker: fitz
text: Deeper doesn't help if there's nowhere lower to go. The ground was so flat and low there was no room to dig them deep enough and keep that slope.

speaker: gauge
text: So the pipes would just sit there? Full?

speaker: fitz
text: Pretty much. So in 1855, the city hired an engineer from Boston, Ellis Chesbrough.

speaker: fitz
text: Chicago became the first big American city to plan a complete sewer system.

speaker: gauge
text: Dig deeper: zero. That was a warm-up.

speaker: fitz
text: Chesbrough's plan flipped the problem. If you can't dig the pipes down, build the street up.

speaker: fitz
text: Workers laid the sewer pipes on top of the existing streets, covered them with earth, and built new streets on top.

speaker: gauge
text: That was going to be my next fix. Sewers on top. Point for Gauge.

speaker: fitz
text: You said "dig deeper" thirty seconds ago.

speaker: gauge
text: And I've grown as a robot.

speaker: fitz
text: Much of that earth was dredged out of the Chicago River itself. The streets went up several feet, up to about ten in places.

speaker: fitz
text: The work started in the late 1850s and went on, street by street, for years.

speaker: gauge
text: But then the buildings are stuck down in a hole.

speaker: fitz
text: That was the catch. So owners jacked their buildings up to match. Sometimes whole blocks at once.

speaker: fitz
text: In 1860 on Lake Street, the paper reported about six thousand screws and six hundred workmen raising a row of buildings about three hundred and twenty feet long.

speaker: fitz
text: On a signal, every man gave each of his screws one quarter turn.

speaker: gauge
text: One quarter turn. I brought a whistle. Did I go up?

speaker: fitz
text: You did not go up.

speaker: fitz
text: But together, that block rose four feet eight inches in five days. The paper said the shops stayed open, and that "not a pane of glass has been broken."

speaker: gauge
text: I broke a glass this morning, and I wasn't lifting anything.

speaker: fitz
text: One of the contractors was George Pullman, later famous for railway sleeping cars. In 1861, his firm raised the Tremont House.

speaker: fitz
text: The Tribune said it rose one foot on the first day, "without a single crack." It had to go up a full six feet.

speaker: fitz
text: And while the work went on, the paper reported, "The business of the Tremont goes on as usual."

speaker: gauge
text: Imagine checking in. "Would you like a room on the ground floor?" "Which ground?"

speaker: fitz
text: The sewers worked. But they drained into the river. And the river flowed into Lake Michigan, the city's drinking water.

speaker: gauge
text: Hold on. So the city drank from the same lake its sewers drained into?

speaker: fitz
text: That's the problem.

speaker: gauge
text: Let's test it. This is Admiral Splash. Go, Admiral.

speaker: gauge
text: Oh no. He's heading straight for the drinking water.

speaker: fitz
text: Exactly. The city's earlier intakes sat within about six hundred feet of shore, pulling in dirty water.

speaker: gauge
text: Then go further out. Fix number three.

speaker: fitz
text: That's what Chesbrough did next. A tunnel under the lake bottom, out to an intake about two miles from shore, protected by a big timber structure called a crib.

speaker: fitz
text: Crews started digging in 1864, by hand, with picks, shovels and mules, twenty-four hours a day, six days a week.

speaker: fitz
text: One crew dug from the shore, another from the far end. In 1866, they met under the lake, lined up to within inches.

speaker: gauge
text: Within inches? I can't find my other sock.

speaker: fitz
text: In 1867, water started flowing in from the crib.

speaker: gauge
text: Point for Gauge. Done.

speaker: fitz
text: Not so fast. When heavy rain flooded the river, its waste still reached the new intake.

speaker: gauge
text: Admiral? How did you get out here?

speaker: gauge
text: Half a point?

speaker: fitz
text: Half a point.

speaker: gauge
text: In 1885, a storm washed sewage into the lake, and an epidemic killed ninety thousand people. That's why they finally acted.

speaker: fitz
text: That story gets repeated a lot. But it didn't happen.

speaker: gauge
text: Wait. Everyone says that.

speaker: fitz
text: Part of it is true. On August second, 1885, a heavy storm hit the city. River historian Libby Hill's research puts it at about five and a half inches of rain in nineteen hours.

speaker: fitz
text: People feared the sewage would reach the water intake.

speaker: fitz
text: But no cholera deaths were reported that year, and typhoid was only slightly above average.

speaker: fitz
text: In 2005, the Chicago Tribune corrected its own earlier stories. It said its archives and public health records showed no such event, and that eighty to ninety thousand deaths would have been far too many to go unnoticed.

speaker: gauge
text: So where did the number come from?

speaker: fitz
text: Nobody is sure. Libby Hill calls it an urban legend.

speaker: gauge
text: I've been telling that one at parties.

speaker: fitz
text: You don't go to parties.

speaker: gauge
text: Robot parties.

speaker: gauge
text: Then what really pushed Chicago to act?

speaker: fitz
text: Something slower. Cholera in 1854 took more than fourteen hundred lives, and typhoid kept coming back for decades.

speaker: fitz
text: The 1885 storm was a frightening scare. But the real reason was decades of waterborne disease, and a river that kept polluting the city's water.

speaker: fitz
text: The real problem was the river. It flowed toward the drinking water.

speaker: gauge
text: Then point the river the other way.

speaker: fitz
text: That's... actually the plan.

speaker: gauge
text: Rivers have a reverse gear?

speaker: fitz
text: West of the city, there's a low ridge. Water on one side drains to the Great Lakes. Water on the other side drains toward the Mississippi.

speaker: fitz
text: A Chicago Public Library history puts it at only about eight feet high.

speaker: gauge
text: Eight feet? That's not a mountain. That's a speed bump.

speaker: fitz
text: So the plan was to dig through it. A canal twenty-eight miles long, from the river's South Branch to Lockport.

speaker: fitz
text: Lake water would flow into the river, carry the sewage away from the lake, and send it down the Des Plaines and Illinois Rivers, toward the Mississippi.

speaker: fitz
text: Illinois created a new agency for the job in 1889, the Sanitary District of Chicago. Digging began in 1892 and took about eight years.

speaker: fitz
text: In January 1900, the district quietly removed a dam at the canal's north end, and the river began to run away from the lake.

speaker: gauge
text: One quarter turn!

speaker: fitz
text: That's two quarter turns.

speaker: gauge
text: Point for Gauge. And everybody downstream was happy?

speaker: fitz
text: Not everyone. St. Louis, downstream on the Mississippi, feared Chicago's sewage would end up in its drinking water. When the canal opened, Missouri asked the U.S. Supreme Court to stop it.

speaker: gauge
text: That's a fair worry, honestly.

speaker: fitz
text: It was. But in 1906, Justice Holmes wrote that Missouri's proof fell far short of what it claimed, and the case was dismissed.

speaker: fitz
text: In the years after the canal, and with chlorine added to the water from 1916, deaths from waterborne disease dropped sharply.

speaker: gauge
text: So it's solved. Case closed?

speaker: fitz
text: Not quite. Even after the reversal, a heavy enough storm could force the district to open the gates and let polluted water out into the lake.

speaker: gauge
text: Admiral, no. We just turned you around.

speaker: fitz
text: Hold onto that. First, though: boats.

speaker: fitz
text: The Chicago River runs right through downtown, and its bridges have to let boats through.

speaker: gauge
text: Make the bridges higher. Boats go under. Fix number... lots.

speaker: fitz
text: Instead, Chicago's bridges move. In the early 1900s, city engineers settled on a design of their own, now called the "Chicago type."

speaker: fitz
text: Each half of the bridge tips up on a huge fixed axle, called a trunnion. Behind the axle sits a heavy counterweight.

speaker: gauge
text: Like a seesaw?

speaker: fitz
text: Exactly like a seesaw. Balanced like that, it takes little power to tip up nearly straight, leaving the whole channel clear.

speaker: fitz
text: The first was the Cortland Street bridge, in 1902: the American Society of Civil Engineers calls it the first of its kind in the United States.

speaker: fitz
text: A 2015 plan for the city counted forty-four movable bridges, thirty-three of which could still open. Most were the Chicago type.

speaker: gauge
text: Higher bridges: no point. Seesaw bridges: that one goes to Chicago.

speaker: fitz
text: Under the Loop, Chicago's downtown, runs an old, long-abandoned network of narrow freight railway tunnels, about forty feet below the streets.

speaker: fitz
text: In 1991, a contractor replaced the wooden pilings that protect the Kinzie Street Bridge. The contractor's drawings didn't show the tunnels.

speaker: fitz
text: The work damaged the roof of one of the old tunnels, right under the river.

speaker: gauge
text: Did anyone notice?

speaker: fitz
text: In January 1992, a cable TV crew reported a leak. The repair was put off for months.

speaker: gauge
text: Put off? With a river on top of it?

speaker: fitz
text: With a river on top of it. On April thirteenth, 1992, the damaged roof gave way. The hole was about as big as a car.

speaker: fitz
text: River water poured into the tunnels, and from there into the basements of hundreds of downtown buildings. An estimated two hundred and fifty million gallons.

speaker: fitz
text: The Loop was evacuated, and power was cut to much of it. No one was hurt.

speaker: gauge
text: Good. Then plug it. With anything. Rocks. Concrete. A very big cork.

speaker: fitz
text: Crews dropped in rock, sand and concrete, then drilled down to place emergency plugs, with the Army Corps of Engineers.

speaker: fitz
text: Most businesses were closed for about three days, some for weeks.

speaker: fitz
text: And some of that water was drained into the Deep Tunnel, which was still being built.

speaker: gauge
text: Plug it: half a point. No cork. And what's the Deep Tunnel?

speaker: fitz
text: Chicago's sewers still follow Chesbrough's design. They're "combined" sewers: the same pipe carries what goes down the toilet and the rain off the street.

speaker: fitz
text: On a dry day, it all goes to treatment plants. In a big storm, the pipes fill up, and the overflow spills into the rivers, or backs up into basements.

speaker: fitz
text: By the 1960s, that was happening on more than a hundred days a year.

speaker: gauge
text: Two pipes. One for rain, one for... the other stuff. Separate every sewer.

speaker: fitz
text: A committee looked at fifty alternatives. Separating every sewer was rejected. It was too costly, too disruptive, and it wouldn't have helped with the flooding.

speaker: gauge
text: Fine. One pipe. But enormous.

speaker: fitz
text: ...Hold that thought.

speaker: fitz
text: In 1972, a plan was chosen. Dig giant tunnels deep in the bedrock, catch the overflow, and store it until the treatment plants can clean it.

speaker: fitz
text: It's called the Tunnel and Reservoir Plan, or the Deep Tunnel. Construction started in 1975, and the tunnels were finished in 2006.

speaker: fitz
text: Today there are about a hundred and ten miles of tunnels, a hundred and fifty to three hundred feet underground, and up to thirty-three feet wide.

speaker: gauge
text: Thirty-three feet wide? So my enormous pipe...

speaker: fitz
text: Honestly? Yes. A very, very big pipe, that holds the storm until the plants catch up.

speaker: fitz
text: The tunnels feed huge reservoirs, including one in an old limestone quarry. The biggest will be the McCook Reservoir, about three hundred feet deep.

speaker: fitz
text: When it's finished, it will hold about ten billion gallons. The district expects that around 2032.

speaker: fitz
text: Overflow days have already dropped from more than a hundred a year to about fifty.

speaker: fitz
text: So, why does Chicago keep fighting its own water?

speaker: fitz
text: Because it was built flat and low, right next to its own drinking water. And every fix solved one problem and uncovered the next.

speaker: gauge
text: Final score. Sewers on top: one. Further out: half. Turn the river around: one. Plug it: half. Enormous pipe: one. Four points!

speaker: fitz
text: Out of eight.

speaker: gauge
text: Four out of eight. ...So what's Chicago's score against the water?

speaker: fitz
text: Still playing.

speaker: gauge
text: And Admiral Splash has retired to a reservoir. Plenty of room.

speaker: fitz
text: If you want to know why the lids on top of all those sewers are round, we made a Short about manhole covers.

speaker: gauge
text: Ooh, what else is built weird? Subscribe and let's find out.
